stem: The volume occupied by a given mass of a gas at 298 K is 25 mL at 1 atmosphere pressure. Calculate the volume of the gas if pressure is increased to 1.25 atmosphere at constant temperature.
solution:
Given : \(\mathrm{P_1} = 1\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 25\ \mathrm{mL}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = 1.25\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = ?\)

According to Boyle's law,

\(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\)

Substituting the values of \(\mathrm{P_1}\), \(\mathrm{V_1}\) and \(\mathrm{P_2}\) in the above expression we get

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} = \dfrac{1 \times 25}{1.25} = 20\ \mathrm{mL}\)

Volume occupied by the gas is 20 mL.
_note: p-09 (printed p.144), left column pink box. The book prints the label as `Problem: 10.1 :` — with a colon AFTER the word Problem — which is why a `Problem 10.` text scan misses it. 10.1 is NOT absent from the book.

stem: At 300 K a certain mass of a gas ocupies \(1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) volume. Calculate its volume at 450 K and at the same pressure.
solution:
Given : \(\mathrm{T_1} = 300\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{V_1} = 1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = 450\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = ?\)

According to Charles' law, at constant pressure,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\qquad \therefore\ \mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{V_1} \times \mathrm{T_2}}{\mathrm{T_1}}\)

\(= \dfrac{450 \times 1 \times 10^{-4}}{300}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{V_2} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
_note: p-10 (printed p.145), right column. `ocupies` is the book's own spelling and is transcribed as printed.

stem: A sample of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas was placed in a flexible 9.0 L container at 300 K at a pressure of 1.5 atm. The gas was compressed to a volume of 3.0 L and heat was added until the temperature reached 600 K. What is the new pressure inside the container?
solution:
Given Data : \(\mathrm{V_1} = 9\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{V_2} = 3\ \mathrm{L}\), \(\mathrm{P_1} = 1.5\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{T_1} = 300\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{T_2} = 600\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{P_2} = ?\)

According to combined gas law equation,

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{T_1}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2V_2}}{\mathrm{T_2}}\)

\(\therefore\ \dfrac{1.5 \times 9}{300} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_2} \times 3}{600}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{P_2} = 9\ \mathrm{atm}\)

stem: Find the temperature in \(^\circ\mathrm{C}\) at which volume and pressure of 1 mol of nitrogen gas becomes \(10\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) and 2.46 atmosphere respectively.
solution:
Given : \(\mathrm{P} = 2.46\ \mathrm{atm}\), \(\mathrm{V} = 10\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(n = 1\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(\mathrm{R} = 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\mathrm{T} = ?\)

Ideal gas equation is

\(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\)

\(\therefore\ \mathrm{T} = \dfrac{\mathrm{PV}}{n\mathrm{R}} = \dfrac{2.46 \times 10}{1 \times 0.0821}\)

\(\mathrm{T} = 299.63\ \mathrm{K}\)

Temp. in \(^\circ\mathrm{C} = 299.63 - 273.15 = 26.48\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
_note: p-13 (printed p.148), right column, below Problem 10.3.

stem: A mixture of 28 g \(\mathrm{N_2}\), 8 g He and 40 g Ne has 20 bar pressure. What is the partial pressure of each of these gases ?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working divides the 40 g of neon by 28 g/mol — nitrogen's molar mass, carried down from the line above — while still printing the quotient as 2 mol. The two cannot both stand, since 40/28 = 1.43. Neon's molar mass is 20 g/mol, which gives exactly 2 mol, and 2 mol is what every later line of the example uses (total 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 mol, mole fraction 2/5, partial pressure 8 bar). The denominator has been corrected to 20 g/mol here so the worked example does not teach the slip; the printed answers 4 bar, 8 bar and 8 bar are unaffected and stand.]

Partial pressure = mole fraction \(\times\) total pressure

**Step 1 :** Determine the number of moles \((n)\) of each gas from its mass \((m)\) and molar mass \((\mathrm{M})\), using the formula \(n = \dfrac{m}{\mathrm{M}}\)

\(n_{\mathrm{N_2}} = \dfrac{28\ \mathrm{g}}{28\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}\)

\(n_{\mathrm{He}} = \dfrac{8\ \mathrm{g}}{4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

\(n_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \dfrac{40\ \mathrm{g}}{20\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Step 2 :** Determine the mole fraction of each gas using the formula \(x = \dfrac{n}{n_{\mathrm{Total}}}\)

\(x_{\mathrm{N_2}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{N_2}}}{n_{\mathrm{N_2}} + n_{\mathrm{He}} + n_{\mathrm{Ne}}} = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{(1 + 2 + 2)\ \mathrm{mol}} = \dfrac{1}{5}\)

\(x_{\mathrm{He}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{He}}}{n_{\mathrm{Total}}} = \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{mol}}{5\ \mathrm{mol}} = \dfrac{2}{5}\)

Similarly \(x_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \dfrac{2}{5}\)

**Step 3 :** Calculate the partial pressure

\(\mathrm{P_{N_2}} = x_{\mathrm{N_2}} \times \mathrm{P_{Total}} = \dfrac{1}{5} \times 20\ \mathrm{bar} = 4\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(\mathrm{P_{He}} = x_{\mathrm{He}} \times \mathrm{P_{Total}} = \dfrac{2}{5} \times 20\ \mathrm{bar} = 8\ \mathrm{bar}\)

\(\mathrm{P_{Ne}} = x_{\mathrm{Ne}} \times \mathrm{P_{Total}} = \dfrac{2}{5} \times 20\ \mathrm{bar} = 8\ \mathrm{bar}\)
_note: p-15 (printed p.150), right column. ⚠ The printed working divides 40 g of Ne by 28 g/mol (neon's molar mass is 20) and still writes 2 mol — 40/28 = 1.43. Transcribed VERBATIM here; corrected via solved-fixes + errata after commit.

subtopic: Liquefaction of Gases and Critical Constants
stem: Water has \(\mathrm{T_c} = 647.1\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(\mathrm{P_c} = 220.6\ \mathrm{bar}\). What do these values imply about the state of water under ordinary conditions?
solution:
[Textbook note (not an error): the book prints the label Problem 10.5 twice — once for the partial-pressure example on printed page 150 and again for this one on printed page 154 — so its worked examples run 10.1, 10.2, 10.3, 10.4, 10.5, 10.5, 10.6, 10.7. This entry keeps the book's own number and adds the suffix b only so that the two questions can be told apart. Nothing in either question or answer is affected.]

The \(\mathrm{T_c}\) and \(\mathrm{P_c}\) values of water are very high compared to the room temperature and common atmosheric pressure. Consequently water exists in liquid state under ordinary condition of temperature and pressure.
_note: p-19 (printed p.154), left column. ⚠ THE BOOK PRINTS THE LABEL `Problem 10.5` A SECOND TIME here — verified on the page image at full size. The ref carries a `b` suffix so the two rows stay distinct while the book's own (defective) numbering stays visible.

subtopic: Liquefaction of Gases and Critical Constants
stem: \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) has \(\mathrm{T_c} = 38.98\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{P_c} = 73\ \mathrm{atm}\). How many phases of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexist at (i) \(50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 73 atm, (ii) \(20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 50 atm.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem gives the critical temperature of carbon dioxide as 38.98 degrees celsius, which contradicts the chapter's own text twice — section 10.7 states that carbon dioxide liquefies at 30.98 degrees celsius and 73 atmosphere, and Table 10.7 lists its critical temperature as 304.10 K, i.e. 30.95 degrees celsius. The correct value is about 30.98 degrees celsius. The stem is preserved exactly as printed because the answers do not depend on which value is used: 50 degrees celsius lies above the critical temperature on either reading and 20 degrees celsius lies below it on either reading, so part (i) is a single phase and part (ii) is two coexisting phases in both cases.]

(i) \(50\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 73 atm represent a condition for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) above its \(\mathrm{T_c}\). Therefore, under this condition \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) exists only as single phase.

(ii) \(20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and 50 atm represent a condition for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) below its \(\mathrm{T_c}\). Therefore, under this condition two phases of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), namely, liquid and gas can coexist.
_note: p-19 (printed p.154), right column. ⚠ The stem's Tc = 38.98 °C contradicts the chapter's own §10.7 text (30.98 °C) and Table 10.7 (304.10 K = 30.95 °C). Both answers hold under either value, so PRESERVED as printed + errata bracket.

stem:
In which of the following cases water will have the highest and the lowest boiling point ?

Water is boiled

a. in an open vessel,

b. in a pressure cooker,

c. in a evacuated vessel.
solution: Higher the pressure to which a liquid is exposed, higher will be its boiling point. The pressure to which water is exposed is maximum in the pressure cooker and minimum in the evacuated vessel. Therefore b.p. of water is highest in (b) and lowest in (c).
